corrected_value.authors: Yang, J., Wang, S., Xu, Y., & Rayner, K.
corrected_value.title: Do chinese readers obtain preview benefit from word n+2? Evidence from eye movements.

decisions.location: Experiment 1, Discussion, page 18, lines 439-446; References, page 44, lines 1089-1091
decisions.quote:
Experiment 1 was an attempt to replicate Yang et al.’s findings, and the analyses on
the regions examined by Yang et al. (i.e., words n, n+1, and n+2) provided a full replication.
Consistent with their findings, we observed n+2 preview effects of 22ms on word n+2 in gaze
duration when word n+1 was high-frequency. Yang et al. (2009) found a marginal (p=0.051)
effect in gaze duration of 22ms, and no effect in other measures. Furthermore, Yang et al.
(2012) did not find any effect of the word n+2 preview when a low-frequency word n+1 was
used. Thus, the pattern of effects was replicated in the current experiment, and our results are
consistent with Yang et al.’s findings.
decisions.reason: Experiment 1 explicitly re-tests the positive word n+2 preview benefit reported in Experiment 2 of Yang, Wang, Xu, and Rayner (2009) (doi:10.1037/a0013554) using its 20 high-frequency word n+1 stimuli, analysed as an independent subset alongside the 20 low-frequency word n+1 stimuli from Yang, Rayner, Li, and Wang (2012) (shipped row input_row_index 1497, doi:10.1007/s11145-010-9282-7). Shipped row 1497 represents only the 2012 low-frequency follow-up study; Yang et al. (2009) is a separate original publication with different authors, stimuli, experimental condition, and empirical finding, so report equivalence does not apply.

decisions.quote:
Before proceeding, we feel it is necessary to explain why we chose to investigate
idioms in the current study, in contrast to the spaced compounds used by Cutter et al. While
we consider both idioms and spaced compounds to fall under the broader category of multi-
word units, they are not without their differences.
decisions.reason: Cutter, Drieghe, and Liversedge (2014) investigated parafoveal preview benefit in English spaced compounds (where word n+1 preview was also manipulated and second-constituent predictability was 97%) and is cited as theoretical motivation and a cross-phenomenon contrast for Experiment 2's novel investigation of three-character Chinese idioms with low within-unit predictability (1.3%). The paper explicitly restricts its empirical replication to Yang et al. (2009) (target_index 0) and Yang et al. (2012) (shipped input_row_index 1497) in Experiment 1, whereas Experiment 2 is a novel extension to Chinese idioms rather than an empirical retest of Cutter et al. (2014).

decisions.quote:
First of all, the terminal word of our items received shorter
fixations when they were part of an idiom as opposed to part of a phrase. This replicates an
effect that has previously been observed in English idioms (see Underwood, Schmitt, &
Galpin, 2004) and translated Chinese idioms (see Carrol & Conklin, 2015). Furthermore,
idioms as a whole received shorter gaze durations than phrases, an effect that has also
previously been observed in English (Siyanova-Chanturia, Conklin, & Schmitt, 2011). More
generally, this pattern of effects supports findings from a range of experimental paradigms
showing that idioms are processed more quickly than phrases. It is worth noting that we
observed these effects despite controlling the relative predictability of the later parts of our
idioms and phrases, which suggests idioms have a special representational status, and this is
not determined by the within idiom predictability. To the best of our knowledge this is the
first study that has shown the idiom processing advantage in natural Chinese reading.
Furthermore, it is also the first to show such effects whilst controlling for potential
predictability effects.
decisions.reason: Underwood, Schmitt, and Galpin (2004) studied English formulaic sequences without controlling final-word predictability and is cited as prior literature background in the Introduction and as a general cross-language literature comparison in the General Discussion. As the authors explicitly state, Experiment 1 conducted the paper's replications (Yang et al., 2009 [target_index 0] and Yang et al., 2012 [shipped input_row_index 1497]), whereas Experiment 2 is a novel study establishing the idiom processing advantage in natural Chinese reading of three-character idioms while controlling predictability.

decisions.quote:
One prior study has used eye-tracking methodology to examine the processing of
Chinese idioms. Carrol and Conklin (2015) presented four-character Chinese idioms, which
were translated into English, to bilingual native Chinese speakers. It was found that the final
word of these translated idioms received shorter fixations than the final word of a matched
phrase. While this study suggests a processing advantage for the final parts of a Chinese
idiom, it remains unclear whether such effects occur during the reading of non-translated
Chinese idioms, and how the characteristics of Chinese text discussed earlier may affect this
process. Also, the focus of the current study was on the processing of three- rather than four-
character Chinese idioms.
decisions.reason: Carrol and Conklin (2015) examined cross-language lexical priming of four-character Chinese idioms translated into English and read in English by bilinguals without controlling predictability. The authors explicitly cite Carrol and Conklin (2015) as background motivation and post-hoc literature comparison for their novel Experiment 2 on non-translated three-character Chinese idioms in natural Chinese reading, whereas actual empirical replication in this paper is confined to Experiment 1 (Yang et al., 2009 [target_index 0] and Yang et al., 2012 [shipped input_row_index 1497]).

decisions.quote:
While we did not observe the expected interaction, we did observe main effects of
phrase type—even though the predictability of the final word of the idiom was controlled—
with idioms being read more quickly than phrases, which indicated an idiom processing
advantage in Chinese over phrases. These results are in line with the findings from English
idioms. For example, Siyanova-Chanturia et al. (2011) found that English idioms were
fixated for a shorter period of time than matched phrases. The results of the current
experiment are also in agreement with findings from decision and naming tasks in three-
character Chinese idioms, in which idioms were responded to faster than matched phrases
(Gu & Liao, 1995; Zhang & Shi, 2009).
decisions.reason: Siyanova-Chanturia, Conklin, and Schmitt (2011) is an English idiom eye-tracking study cited as background literature and post-hoc cross-language consistency alongside Chinese decision and naming studies (Gu & Liao, 1995; Zhang & Shi, 2009) when discussing Experiment 2's novel Chinese idiom reading results. Only Yang et al. (2009) (target_index 0) and Yang et al. (2012) (shipped input_row_index 1497) in Experiment 1 are empirically retested replication targets.

corrected_value.authors: Burke BL, Martens A, Faucher EH
corrected_value.title: Two decades of terror management theory: a meta-analysis of mortality salience research

decisions.location: Introduction, lines 12-16; Discussion, lines 38 and 40; Authors' contributions, line 51; References, lines 65-69
decisions.quote: Overall, the pattern of results reported in the previous section are inconsistent with the original results of Goldenberg et al. [9]. This does not necessarily mean that the original effect was a false positive, but it does suggest that (i) the effect may be substantially smaller than originally reported or (ii) that the effect is extremely sensitive to contextual factors and perhaps absent in some populations. Consistent with the former interpretation, our own reanalysis of Burke et al. ([3]; see also [11]) provides compelling evidence that the effect sizes of previous research on mortality salience may have been overestimated.
decisions.reason: In addition to conducting a new-sample laboratory replication of Goldenberg et al. (2001) Study 2 (shipped input_row_index 1093, doi:10.1037/0096-3445.130.3.427), the authors perform and report their own original-data reanalysis of the 277 mortality-salience effect sizes from the meta-analysis of Burke, Martens, and Faucher (2010) (doi:10.1177/1088868309352321) in Figure 1 and lines 13-16, converting correlations to Fisher's z scores, testing funnel-plot asymmetry with Egger's regression (z = 2.06, p = 0.039), and fitting a Vevea and Hedges selection model (chi2(1) = 47.87, p < 0.001; bias-corrected r = 0.22 vs Burke et al.'s r = 0.35). Shipped row 1093 covers only the Goldenberg et al. (2001) experiment, so Burke et al. (2010) is a genuinely absent reproduction target.
